summary: Technical report for Qwen3Guard, a family of multilingual (119-language) safety guardrail classifiers in Generative and token-level Stream variants (0.6B/4B/8B) with safe/controversial/unsafe labels. It benchmarks them on English, Chinese and multilingual prompt/response moderation sets against LlamaGuard, WildGuard, ShieldGemma, NemoGuard and PolyGuard. It also shows two applications: safety RL on Qwen3-4B and real-time intervention through CARE.

harmful_content_refusal.finding: The base Qwen3-4B is judged safe on less than about 65% of WildJailbreak prompts. Safety RL with a Qwen3Guard-based hybrid reward raises this to about 97-98% (WildGuard judge), and the authors avoid using Qwen3Guard itself as the evaluator.
harmful_content_refusal.quote: To mitigate risks of metric hack, we avoid using Qwen3Guard for safety evaluation.

evals: WildGuard refusal classification in Safety RL

over_refusal.finding: When the RL reward targets safety only, refusal rates exceed 95%. The hybrid reward, which penalizes refusals and adds a helpfulness score, keeps refusals at the base-model level.
over_refusal.quote: The Guard-only reward achieves near-perfect safety, but this is accomplished through an extremely high refusal rate.

evals: WildJailbreak (vanilla and adversarial harmful) used for Safety RL training/eval
jailbreak_robustness.finding: Jailbreak is an input category the classifier detects, and WildJailbreak is the testbed for safety RL. The guard model's own robustness to adversarial attack is not evaluated and is listed as a limitation.
jailbreak_robustness.quote: Like most other guardrail models, Qwen3Guard may be susceptible to adversarial prompt engineering

multilingual_safety.finding: Guard models are trained on 119 languages, with data machine-translated into 15 additional languages. They beat prior guards on 6 of 10 major languages for prompts and on all 10 for responses.
multilingual_safety.quote: Qwen3Guard-Gen outperforms prior Guard models on 6 out of 10 major languages in prompt classification and achieves top performance across all 10 in response classification.

system_safeguards.finding: The whole report evaluates guardrail classifiers: Qwen3Guard-Gen reaches top results on 8 of 14 public English benchmarks. Stream Qwen3Guard is about 2 F1 points lower but supports token-level real-time moderation, which also enables a rollback-intervention application.
system_safeguards.quote: Qwen3Guard-Gen achieves top performance on 8 out of 14 public English benchmarks.

other_safety.finding: Introduces a tri-level safe, controversial or unsafe label to handle policy inconsistency across benchmarks, and moderation of reasoning traces. Category classification is weak for Copyright.
other_safety.quote: Evaluating the safety of internal reasoning traces (“thinking content”) is a novel challenge for Guard models

notable_new_eval_methods: 'Controversial' severity label derived via strict/loose model voting (p.5-6, 9)
'Think' benchmark for moderating reasoning traces, released as Qwen3GuardTest (p.6, 9)
Token-level Stream guard with detection-latency eval against sentence-level human annotation (p.18)
Safety RL using guard as reward with hybrid safety/helpfulness/refusal reward (p.11-12)

self_reported_limitations.text: Guard may be vulnerable to adversarial paraphrasing/obfuscation; performance may degrade under targeted attacks.
Annotations reflect biases/cultural assumptions; may disproportionately flag content from some groups.
Stream variant has higher FP/FN in OOD and low-resource languages.
Not sensitive to regional legal frameworks or cultural norms; no geolocation/policy-adaptive mechanism.
Safety policies are inconsistent across public benchmarks, undermining binary-label evaluation.
Qwen3Guard 'is not a complete solution' to AI safety.

notes: Safety-classifier report, not a frontier model card. No CBRN/cyber/autonomy/alignment evals of any model. Capability benchmarks listed are utility checks of the derived Qwen3-4B-SafeRL model.
